doc.title: John Best interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Bobby Hackett's String of Pearls solo
summary: How Hackett filled in the solo that Miller arrangements later wrote out.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Tell me about, was it Bobby Hacket that played that trumpet solo on, I think it was “String of Pearls.”
You were on that record, yeah.
Did he just improvise that on the spot?
It sounds like, it’s such a nice solo, it almost sounds like someone sat down and wrote it out.

Glenn, it was a Billy May solo with a plunger. And it didn’t seem to fit the background. The trombones have a little background. So Glenn said, “Hey Bobby” — Bobby’s playing guitar — he said, “You think you could fill in on that?” And he did and that’s what came out. Bobby was a beautiful player, just great. And he knew chords and of course he was a guitar player. But he had excellent taste to me. I mean he belongs in the Teagarden class. He couldn’t play the horn like Berigan, but what he did was just beautiful.
Now it’s interesting because if you buy the Glenn Miller arrangement of that song, they have his solo written out.
It’s like it’s so perfect you have to do it.

Yeah. I had to play it a lot of times. Well, I worked with Tex quite a bit, and the Modernaires and went out together as a thing, and that was it, but most people, they don’t play it note for note, unless you’re on a stage or something, then they will play it. But if you’re on a dance job, they don’t.
